# 7. The within-plex permutation null {#nulls}

## 7a. Why `fgsea`'s own p-value cannot be used here {#why-not-fgsea}

`fgsea`'s null asks how often a *random set of the same size* drawn from this
ranking is as enriched. That treats COG O's 405 proteins as 405 independent
pieces of evidence. They are not: they were measured in the same 55 samples,
many come from the same organisms, and they share plex and normalisation
effects. If a few non-responder samples carry more chaperone — through biology,
a plex offset, or one bacterium blooming — all 405 move together. Random sets
essentially never do, so the p-value comes out astronomically small, and
smaller the larger the set. Fifty-five rooms with 405 thermometers each are 55
observations, not 22,275.

The label permutation asks the study's question instead: if response were
unrelated to the proteome in these 55 patients, how often would the set look
this enriched? Everything that makes proteins move together is preserved; only
the label-to-sample link is broken.

**Measured, across 30 sets and 1,000 draws:** the permutation null's SD has
median **1.144** (range 0.979–1.409) rather than 1, and its location is
displaced. The gap this opens:

| set | `fgsea` internal p | within-plex permutation p |
|---|---|---|
| COG O | 2.8 × 10⁻¹⁶ | **`r vc("p.O", "0.006")`** |
| COG O ∩ chaperones | 6.7 × 10⁻²⁰ | **`r vc("p.Ochap", "0.003")`** |

More `fgsea` permutations do not help — they estimate the wrong null more
precisely. This is the inter-gene-correlation problem that made the original
GSEA permute sample labels, and one measured feature worsens it here: response
is unevenly spread across plexes (§0), so whole blocks of the ranking move
together.

## 7b. Building the null input

Self-contained: no external-drive paths, no metagenomics. The observed NES is
recomputed inside the null script from the same sets, so the two cannot drift.

```{r null-prep}
## Pittsburgh's null input. Its Sheba part (KEEP_S = mixtures 3-5, MS2) is the
## input of the superseded Sheba design; the primary is built by prep_sheba_pooled.R.
KEEP_P <- arm_mix_v13("pitt_ontx")
KEEP_S <- arm_mix_v13("sheba_ontx")
stopifnot(length(KEEP_P) == 6L)

save(qf, SAMP_PRIMARY, PARAMS, RESP_LEVELS, SETS_P, SETS_S, KEEP_P, KEEP_S,
     fit_arm, pick_denom, arm_mix_v13,
     file = file.path(paths$out_dir, "null_input.RData"), compress = "xz")
## The design these draws must be made on (13 Oct 2026). run_null_2026-10-13.R
## writes the same string into the draws directory from the qf it loads, and the
## scoring chunks below refuse a directory whose design differs.
writeLines(pitt_design_id(OP$d$sample), file.path(paths$out_dir, "null_design_pitt.txt"))
file.size(file.path(paths$out_dir, "null_input.RData")) / 1e6
tools::md5sum(file.path(paths$out_dir, "null_input.RData"))
## MEASURED 23 Sep 2026, restored pipeline: 30.96 MB,
## md5 de030e223f0b0232d07cb88bb6e84ef0.
##
## THAT CHECKSUM IS A DATED RECORD, NOT THIS FILE'S IDENTITY. The input is
## rewritten whenever the design moves, and it has moved since: the size stays
## at 30.96 MB while the md5 does not, so a size check cannot see the
## difference and a checksum comparison against the line above will fail on any
## current file. The 23 Sep value records what the §7e restoration check
## consumed, and nothing else. What identifies a current input is the design
## stamp written beside it (null_design_pitt.txt, above) and refused by the
## scoring chunks when it differs -- that mechanism exists precisely because
## file identity stopped being stable here.
##
## Contents verified against the record: SETS_P at O 405, O_chap 324,
## chaperones 393, O_chap_noGD 157, O_remainder 81, ribosomal 928; SETS_S 28.
##
## KEEP_P = 6 and KEEP_S = 3 are MIXTURES, not samples — Pittsburgh's six usable
## plexes (TMT2 at 9 NR / 1 R and TMT5 at 0 NR / 10 R fail the 2/2 rule) and
## Sheba's three on-treatment mixtures 3, 4 and 5 (mixture 2 contributes a single
## channel and fails it). That is why OS$d is 29 = 10 + 10 + 9.
##
## NOTE what the next chunk does and does not test. `score-pitt-nulls` scores the
## ARCHIVED draws, so reproducing NES -2.24 / p 0.006 / q 0.045 verifies the
## scoring code against inputs it always had. It does not exercise the fit or the
## permutation. End-to-end verification of the null needs a fresh short run from
## THIS file, scored against the archived observed values.
```

For Sheba's pre-specified primary the input is built by `prep_sheba_pooled.R`,
which pools mixtures 1, 3, 4 and 5 at **patient** level (n = 35) and asserts the
per-plex R/NR table before writing.

## 7c. `run_null.R` — the engine behind every enrichment p

One `.rds` per draw, so a run is resumable and nothing accumulates in memory.

**Superseded as of 13 October 2026.** The file to run is
`run_null_2026-10-13.R`, which is this worker plus the design stamp §7d's
scoring chunks require, and two abort-early guards on the number of analysed
samples and the number of gene sets in the input. The listing below is kept as
the record of what produced the archived draws; do not run it.

```r
## LISTING ONLY — this is the server worker, not document code. It reads
## commandArgs() and writes one .rds per draw. Shown here as the record of what
## produced the null archives; it must never run inside the analysis session, so
## the fence below is plain `r` rather than an executable chunk.
#!/usr/bin/env Rscript
## 1,000-draw within-plex permutation null. One .rds per draw.
## Usage: Rscript run_null.R <cohort> <first_draw> <last_draw> <outdir>
args <- commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE)
COH <- args[1]; D1 <- as.integer(args[2]); D2 <- as.integer(args[3])
OUT <- args[4]; dir.create(OUT, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
stopifnot(COH %in% c("pitt", "sheba"))

## LOAD ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING: Bioconductor first, tidyverse last.
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(QFeatures); library(msqrob2); library(SummarizedExperiment)
  library(fgsea); library(MsCoreUtils)
  library(tibble); library(tidyr); library(purrr); library(dplyr)
})
stopifnot(environmentName(environment(dplyr::count)) == "dplyr")

load("null_input.RData")
Q    <- qf[[COH]]
SETS <- if (COH == "pitt") SETS_P else SETS_S
KEEP <- if (COH == "pitt") KEEP_P else KEEP_S

## ---- observed, recomputed here so it cannot drift from the null ----------
fit_and_score <- function(q) {
  f  <- fit_arm(q, KEEP, "perm")
  st <- setNames(f$res$t, f$res$feature); st <- st[is.finite(st)]
  fgseaMultilevel(SETS, st, minSize = 10, maxSize = 2000, eps = 0) |>
    tibble::as_tibble() |> dplyr::select(pathway, size, NES)
}
obs_f <- file.path(OUT, paste0("observed_", COH, ".rds"))
if (!file.exists(obs_f)) saveRDS(fit_and_score(Q), obs_f)

## ---- permutation ---------------------------------------------------------
## Shuffle resp WITHIN Mixture, among the samples the fit will actually use.
perm_resp <- function(q, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  cd <- as.data.frame(colData(q))
  use <- !cd$is_norm & !cd$excluded & !is.na(cd$resp) & cd$Mixture %in% KEEP
  r <- as.character(cd$resp)
  r[use] <- ave(r[use], droplevels(factor(cd$Mixture[use])), FUN = sample)
  colData(q)$resp <- factor(r, levels = RESP_LEVELS)
  q
}

for (i in D1:D2) {
  f <- file.path(OUT, sprintf("null_%s_%04d.rds", COH, i))
  if (file.exists(f)) next                       # resumable
  t0 <- Sys.time()
  res <- tryCatch(fit_and_score(perm_resp(Q, 10000L + i)),
                  error = function(e) { message("draw ", i, ": ", conditionMessage(e)); NULL })
  if (!is.null(res)) saveRDS(dplyr::mutate(res, draw = i), f)
  message(sprintf("%s draw %d  %.1f min", COH, i,
                  as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), t0, units = "mins"))))
}
```

Run `run_null_2026-10-13.R`, not the listing above, and pass the two expected
counts — 55 analysed samples and 30 sets for the reported run — so a wrong input
stops in a minute rather than after a thousand draws. Draw 1 alone first: it
writes `design.txt` and `observed_pitt.rds`, which sixteen workers would race.

```bash
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1
mkdir -p logs
Rscript run_null_2026-10-13.R pitt 1 1 nulls_pitt null_input.RData 55 30
seq 2 1000 | xargs -P 16 -I{} sh -c \
  'Rscript run_null_2026-10-13.R pitt {} {} nulls_pitt null_input.RData 55 30 > logs/draw_{}.log 2>&1'
```

## 7d. Scoring

Draws in which a set cannot be scored are reported explicitly, and the
multiplicity correction is given both dropping them (`q_drop`) and counting
them as exceedances (`q_cons`). Pittsburgh's null is 1,000 draws. The Monte
Carlo intervals of the four result-carrying p-values exclude 0.05 (second chunk
below); COG K's (p = 0.053) includes it, and K is not claimed. Extension to
10,000 draws is Sheba's pre-specified rule (§12c).

The same draws also support a **family-wise** correction over the 30 sets, which
is stricter than BH: the per-draw maximum |NES| across the family is the
Westfall–Young null. Its median is 1.79 and its maximum 2.65, so COG O ∩
chaperones (0.009) and chaperones (0.013) clear it while COG O (0.055) and the
set without GroEL and DnaK (0.058) fall just outside. The same matrix gives the family's dependence, and it is
not what the headline number suggests: the nested sets correlate at 0.87 to 0.97
across draws, while the mean over all 435 pairs is 0.024 because 24 unrelated COG
categories dominate the count and cancel in sign. Effective-test estimators
assume one common correlation and do not apply. Max-T needs no such assumption,
which is why it is the quoted correction. Note also that COG O itself sits at
0.055, outside FWER, and is Sheba's pre-specified primary (§12c). Neither
addresses the selection of the 30 sets, which is §13 item 9.

```{r null-design-check}
## 13 Oct 2026. Draws made on one sample set cannot be scored against an observed
## statistic from another, and nothing in the draws themselves would show it: the
## files and the code are identical, only the design moved. The corrected design
## (55 analysed samples, after two retracted intermediates) invalidates every draw, so the
## scoring chunks run only on a directory stamped with the current design by
## run_null_2026-10-13.R. Archive the old directories; do not delete them.
NULL_DESIGN <- pitt_design_id(OP$d$sample)
draws_ok <- function(dir) {
  f <- file.path(dir, "design.txt")
  file.exists(f) && identical(readLines(f, warn = FALSE)[1], NULL_DESIGN)
}
NULLS_PITT_OK <- draws_ok(file.path(paths$out_dir, "nulls_pitt"))
if (!NULLS_PITT_OK)
  warning("nulls_pitt/ is absent or was generated on a different sample set. ",
          "The permutation p-values in sections 7d-7e are NOT computed in this run. ",
          "Generate draws from null_input.RData with run_null_2026-10-13.R and re-knit.",
          call. = FALSE)
c(analysed_samples = nrow(OP$d), nulls_pitt_match_design = NULLS_PITT_OK)
```

```{r score-pitt-nulls, eval = isTRUE(get0("NULLS_PITT_OK"))}
score_nulls <- function(dir, coh) {
  obs <- as.data.frame(readRDS(file.path(dir, sprintf("observed_%s.rds", coh))))
  fs  <- list.files(dir, sprintf("^null_%s_\\d+\\.rds$", coh), full.names = TRUE)   # \\d{4} missed draw 10000
  nl  <- do.call(rbind, lapply(fs, function(f) as.data.frame(readRDS(f))))
  out <- do.call(rbind, lapply(obs$pathway, function(pw) {
    x <- nl$NES[nl$pathway == pw]; o <- obs$NES[obs$pathway == pw]
    xv <- x[!is.na(x)]; ex <- sum(abs(xv) >= abs(o)); nNA <- sum(is.na(x))
    data.frame(pathway = pw, NES = o, n_valid = length(xv), n_NA = nNA, exceed = ex,
               null_sd = sd(xv), frac_neg = mean(xv < 0),
               p_drop = (1 + ex) / (1 + length(xv)),          # NA draws dropped
               p_cons = (1 + ex + nNA) / (1 + length(x)))     # NA draws counted as exceeding
  }))
  out$q_drop <- p.adjust(out$p_drop, "BH"); out$q_cons <- p.adjust(out$p_cons, "BH")
  out[order(out$p_drop), ]
}
sp <- score_nulls(file.path(paths$out_dir, "nulls_pitt"), "pitt")
vc_put("p.O", spv("O", "p_drop")); vc_put("p.Ochap", spv("O_chap", "p_drop"))
print(sp[, c("pathway", "NES", "null_sd", "frac_neg", "p_drop", "q_drop",
             "p_cons", "q_cons")], row.names = FALSE)
```

**The permutation null is neither centered nor unit-variance**, measured rather
than assumed: across the `r v(nrow(sp), "30")` Pittsburgh sets its standard
deviation runs `r v(min(sp$null_sd), "0.98")` to `r v(max(sp$null_sd), "1.41")`,
median `r v(stats::median(sp$null_sd), "1.14")`, and the fraction of draws below
zero runs `r v(min(sp$frac_neg), "0.40")` to `r v(max(sp$frac_neg), "0.615")`.
<!-- The maximum is exactly 0.615, sitting on the two-decimal rounding boundary:
     R prints 0.61 (the nearest double is 0.6149999...), decimal round-half-up
     gives 0.62, which is what Methods carries and what an inclusive upper bound
     should be. Recorded at three decimals here so the site is exact and stops
     reporting a DRIFT that is a rounding convention rather than a stale number.
     Methods needs no change. -->
This is the sentence Methods carries. It had no site here until 14 Oct, which is
why the 55-channel run checked the standard deviations only by eye and the
fraction below zero not at all.

```{r pitt-mc-intervals, eval = isTRUE(get0("NULLS_PITT_OK"))}
## ADDED in the 22 September audit, not part of the original run: Monte Carlo
## 95% intervals from the recorded exceedance counts (the scorer above does not
## compute them). Checked against nulls_scored_pitt_2026-09-21.csv.
mc <- t(vapply(seq_len(nrow(sp)), function(i)
  binom.test(sp$exceed[i], sp$n_valid[i])$conf.int, numeric(2)))
sp$mc_lo <- mc[, 1]; sp$mc_hi <- mc[, 2]
sp[sp$pathway %in% c("O", "O_chap", "chaperones", "O_chap_noGD", "K"),
   c("pathway", "p_drop", "mc_lo", "mc_hi")]

## sp is complete only here -- mc_lo/mc_hi are attached above, the scorer does not
## compute them. Written out because score_nulls() kept the scored table in memory
## only: after the 14 Oct run the sole way back to the exceedance counts was to
## invert p_drop = (1+exceed)/(1+n_valid) from the printed digits. One CSV ends that.
write.csv(sp, file.path(paths$out_dir, "nulls_scored_pitt.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

## The two claims Methods makes about these intervals, COMPUTED rather than typed.
## An `## EXPECTED` block here carried the September numbers and every one of the
## five went stale on the 14 Oct run; a printed verdict cannot go stale.
.res <- c("O", "O_chap", "chaperones", "O_chap_noGD")
.i   <- match(.res, sp$pathway); .w <- sp$mc_hi[.i] - sp$mc_lo[.i]; .k <- match("K", sp$pathway)
cat(sprintf("  result-carrying sets whose interval excludes 0.05: %d of %d%s\n",
            sum(sp$mc_hi[.i] < 0.05), length(.res),
            if (all(sp$mc_hi[.i] < 0.05)) "" else "   <-- METHODS CLAIM BROKEN"))
cat(sprintf("  widest of those: %s, %.3f to %.3f\n",
            .res[which.max(.w)], sp$mc_lo[.i][which.max(.w)], sp$mc_hi[.i][which.max(.w)]))
cat(sprintf("  COG K: p %.3f, interval %.3f to %.3f, includes 0.05: %s%s\n",
            sp$p_drop[.k], sp$mc_lo[.k], sp$mc_hi[.k],
            sp$mc_lo[.k] <= 0.05 && sp$mc_hi[.k] >= 0.05,
            if (sp$mc_lo[.k] <= 0.05 && sp$mc_hi[.k] >= 0.05) "" else "   <-- METHODS CLAIM BROKEN"))
```

```{r pitt-westfall-young, eval = isTRUE(get0("NULLS_PITT_OK"))}
## ADDED 23 September, from the archived draws rather than a new run: the
## per-draw NES matrix already carries the family's dependence structure.
fs <- list.files(file.path(paths$out_dir, "nulls_pitt"), "^null_pitt_[0-9]+\\.rds$",
                 full.names = TRUE)
nl <- do.call(rbind, lapply(fs, function(f) as.data.frame(readRDS(f))))
obs <- as.data.frame(readRDS(file.path(paths$out_dir, "nulls_pitt", "observed_pitt.rds")))
M <- reshape(nl[, c("draw", "pathway", "NES")], idvar = "draw", timevar = "pathway",
             direction = "wide")
rownames(M) <- M$draw; M <- as.matrix(M[, -1]); colnames(M) <- sub("^NES\\.", "", colnames(M))
M <- M[, obs$pathway[obs$pathway %in% colnames(M)], drop = FALSE]

mx <- apply(abs(M), 1, max, na.rm = TRUE)          # Westfall-Young null
data.frame(pathway = obs$pathway, NES = obs$NES,
           p_wy = vapply(abs(obs$NES), function(o)
             (1 + sum(mx >= o, na.rm = TRUE)) / (1 + sum(is.finite(mx))), 0)) |>
  (\(d) d[order(d$p_wy, -abs(d$NES)), ])() |> head(6)

C  <- cor(M, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")        # how dependent is the family?
ev <- eigen(C, symmetric = TRUE)$values; ev <- ev[ev > 0]; m <- ncol(C)
for (pr in list(c("O","O_chap"), c("O","chaperones"), c("O_chap","chaperones"),
                c("O","O_chap_noGD"), c("O_chap","O_chap_noGD")))
  if (all(pr %in% colnames(C)))
    cat(sprintf("  nested %-24s r = %+.3f\n", paste(pr, collapse=" ~ "), C[pr[1], pr[2]]))
c(mean_r_all_pairs = mean(C[upper.tri(C)]),
  cheverud_nyholt = 1 + (m - 1) * (1 - var(ev) / m),
  li_ji = sum(ifelse(ev >= 1, 1, 0) + (ev - floor(ev))),
  variance_ratio = m / (1 + (m - 1) * mean(C[upper.tri(C)])))
## EXPECTED: 1,000 draws x 30 sets, 33 draws with an NA. max|NES| median 1.79,
##   95th 2.25, max 2.65. p_wy: O_chap 0.009, chaperones 0.013, O 0.055,
##   O_chap_noGD 0.058; 2 of 30 sets below 0.05. mean_r 0.024; effective tests
##   28.3 (Cheverud-Nyholt), 21.0 (Li-Ji), 17.6 (variance ratio) — reported for
##   completeness only: they assume one common correlation, which is false here.
##   Nested pairs: O~O_chap 0.944, O~chaperones 0.926, O_chap~chaperones 0.970,
##   O~O_chap_noGD 0.865, O_chap~O_chap_noGD 0.880. The mean over all 435 pairs
##   (0.024) is dominated by 24 unrelated COG categories and cancels in sign.
```

## 7e. Does the restored pipeline generate the same null? {#restoration-check}

```{r restoration-null-check, eval = FALSE}
## RECORD (13 Oct 2026): validated the restored pipeline on the 55-sample design of
## September; its draws do not apply to the corrected design.
## 50 draws generated on the server from the null_input.RData this document
## wrote on 23 Sep (md5 de030e22..., a dated record -- see the note at
## `null-prep`), scored against the archived 1,000-draw null. This is
## the ONLY test that exercises the restored fit and permutation rather than the
## scoring code: `score-pitt-nulls` reads archived draws and would reproduce the
## recorded values whatever happened upstream.
EXT <- file.path(paths$out_dir, "nulls_pitt_ext")
if (dir.exists(EXT)) {
  rd <- function(d) do.call(rbind, lapply(
    list.files(d, "^null_pitt_[0-9]+\\.rds$", full.names = TRUE),
    function(f) as.data.frame(readRDS(f))))
  new <- rd(EXT); old <- rd(file.path(paths$out_dir, "nulls_pitt"))
  obs <- as.data.frame(readRDS(file.path(EXT, "observed_pitt.rds")))
  sets_both <- intersect(unique(new$pathway), unique(old$pathway))
  ks <- vapply(sets_both, function(p) suppressWarnings(
    ks.test(new$NES[new$pathway == p], old$NES[old$pathway == p])$p.value), 0)
  cat(sprintf("%d draws against %d; KS p < 0.05 in %d of %d sets (expect ~%.1f)\n",
              dplyr::n_distinct(new$draw), dplyr::n_distinct(old$draw),
              sum(ks < .05), length(ks), .05 * length(ks)))
  print(data.frame(set = sets_both, ks_p = round(ks, 3))[order(ks), ][1:6, ], row.names = FALSE)
} else message("nulls_pitt_ext not present; see nulls_pitt_ext_2026-09-23.zip")
## EXPECTED: 50 against 1,000 draws; 0 of 30 sets at KS p < 0.05. Null SDs agree
## (O 1.334 / 1.340, O_chap 1.415 / 1.409, chaperones 1.384 / 1.394, ribosomal
## 1.332 / 1.355) and means sit near zero in both. All four result sets have no
## draw exceeding the observed, so p = 0.020 is the 50-draw resolution floor and
## is consistent with the archive's 0.003 to 0.026. The run log records
## "observed identical to archived: TRUE" and a pre-flight of 55 samples across
## 6 plexes with 6,939 of 8,478 estimable — matching `fit-both`.
##
## This verifies the fit, the permutation and the null. It does NOT touch the
## universe discrepancy in §6a: the null runs on SETS_P, which is built from
## names(stat) and reproduced exactly, not on univ.
```

---

# 8. The chaperone result — Pittsburgh {#chaperone}

## 8a. What it is

In Pittsburgh, sampled on treatment, **COG category O is enriched toward
non-responders, carried by its chaperone members.** Under the 1,000-draw
within-plex null:

| set | size | NES | p | q (BH, 30 sets) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **COG O** | `r v(szp("O"), "405")` | **`r v(spv("O","NES"), "-2.24")`** | **`r v(spv("O","p_drop"), "0.006")`** | **`r v(spv("O","q_drop"), "0.045")`** (`r v(spv("O","q_cons"), "0.100")` counting NA draws) |
| **COG O ∩ chaperones** | `r v(szp("O_chap"), "324")` | **`r v(spv("O_chap","NES"), "-2.46")`** | **`r v(spv("O_chap","p_drop"), "0.003")`** | **`r v(spv("O_chap","q_drop"), "0.045")`** |
| **chaperones** | `r v(szp("chaperones"), "393")` | **`r v(spv("chaperones","NES"), "-2.43")`** | **`r v(spv("chaperones","p_drop"), "0.004")`** | **`r v(spv("chaperones","q_drop"), "0.045")`** |
| COG O ∩ chaperones, without GroEL/DnaK | `r v(szp("O_chap_noGD"), "157")` | `r v(spv("O_chap_noGD","NES"), "-2.23")` | `r v(spv("O_chap_noGD","p_drop"), "0.026")` | `r v(spv("O_chap_noGD","q_drop"), "0.156")` |
| COG O remainder | `r v(szp("O_remainder"), "81")` | +`r v(spv("O_remainder","NES"), "0.79")` | `r v(spv("O_remainder","p_drop"), "0.891")` | `r v(spv("O_remainder","q_drop"), "0.978")` |
| COG K | `r v(szp("K"), "200")` | `r v(spv("K","NES"), "-1.60")` | `r v(spv("K","p_drop"), "0.053")` | `r v(spv("K","q_drop"), "0.227")` |
| ribosomal | `r v(szp("ribosomal"), "928")` | `r v(spv("ribosomal","NES"), "-1.77")` | `r v(spv("ribosomal","p_drop"), "0.093")` | `r v(spv("ribosomal","q_drop"), "0.278")` |
| COG D | `r v(szp("D"), "127")` | `r v(spv("D","NES"), "-1.37")` | `r v(spv("D","p_drop"), "0.137")` | `r v(spv("D","q_drop"), "0.355")` |
| COG J | `r v(szp("J"), "1341", big=TRUE)` | `r v(spv("J","NES"), "-1.47")` | `r v(spv("J","p_drop"), "0.157")` | `r v(spv("J","q_drop"), "0.362")` |

Two readings follow. The enrichment is **carried by the chaperone members** —
the `r v(szp("O_remainder"), "81")`-protein remainder is flat and positive. And the evidence narrows toward
GroEL and DnaK without excluding the rest: without them, COG O's chaperones still
rank at NES `r v(spv("O_chap_noGD","NES"), "-2.23")`, as strong as COG O itself, but at `r v(szp("O_chap_noGD"), "157")` proteins the null is
wider and they clear only nominally (p = `r v(spv("O_chap_noGD","p_drop"), "0.026")`, q = `r v(spv("O_chap_noGD","q_drop"), "0.156")`). §8e shows the same
split by abundance.

**COG G is not a finding.** It reaches q = `r v(spv("G","q_drop"), "0.045")` (NES +`r v(spv("G","NES"), "1.41")`, R-up) in this
specification, but reverses sign when the plex term is removed, as metabolic
categories do in this design (§4a).

## 8b. Specificity checks

Leading-edge composition; peptide support; removal of the chaperone members; a
Bacillota-internal denominator; a size- and detection-matched random-set
control; set comparability between cohorts; the host–microbe association;
phylum fractions; a within-genus chaperone fraction.

Each recorded result below is labelled with the annotation and taxonomy it was
measured on.

```{r c1-leading-edge}
## KO composition of each cohort's COG O leading edge (le_P / le_S, §6c).
le_ko <- function(le, coh) {
  annot |> dplyr::filter(cohort == coh, protein %in% le) |>
    dplyr::count(ko_primary, sort = TRUE) |>
    dplyr::mutate(cohort = coh, frac = n / sum(n))
}
LE_P <- le_ko(le_P, "pitt"); LE_S <- le_ko(le_S, "sheba")

dplyr::full_join(LE_P |> dplyr::select(ko_primary, n_pitt = n, frac_pitt = frac),
                 LE_S |> dplyr::select(ko_primary, n_sheba = n, frac_sheba = frac),
                 by = "ko_primary") |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(dplyr::coalesce(n_pitt, 0L) +
                             dplyr::coalesce(n_sheba, 0L))) |> as.data.frame()
```

```{r c1b-peptide-support}
## Is the leading edge skewed on peptide support relative to its parent set?
le_support <- function(le, set_prots, coh) {
  annot |> dplyr::filter(cohort == coh, protein %in% set_prots) |>
    dplyr::mutate(in_le = protein %in% le) |>
    dplyr::group_by(in_le) |>
    dplyr::summarise(n = dplyr::n(),
                     median_npep = median(n_peptides, na.rm = TRUE),
                     frac_single = mean(n_peptides == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
                     median_len  = median(length, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    dplyr::mutate(cohort = coh)
}
dplyr::bind_rows(le_support(le_P, sets$COG$O,   "pitt"),
                 le_support(le_S, sets_s$COG$O, "sheba")) |> as.data.frame()

## Effect size vs precision — the discriminating comparison. If Huber weighting
## drove edge membership, `se` would separate as strongly as |logFC|.
dplyr::bind_rows(
  FA$res |> dplyr::filter(feature %in% sets$COG$O)   |>
    dplyr::mutate(in_le = feature %in% le_P, cohort = "pitt"),
  FS$res |> dplyr::filter(feature %in% sets_s$COG$O) |>
    dplyr::mutate(in_le = feature %in% le_S, cohort = "sheba")) |>
  dplyr::group_by(cohort, in_le) |>
  dplyr::summarise(n = dplyr::n(), median_se = median(se),
                   median_abs_lfc = median(abs(logFC)), .groups = "drop") |>
  as.data.frame()
```

```{r c2-chaperone-removal}
## CHAPERONE_KO is defined in §1b. Uses chap_new (§5c), NOT chap_prot: this
## chunk runs after the re-annotation and pep_ph here is already the completed
## taxonomy, so taking the chaperone set from the initial annotation mixed two
## vintages in one statistic. Switched 23 Sep 2026.
O_nochap <- setdiff(sets$COG$O, chap_new)
O_chap   <- intersect(sets$COG$O, chap_new)
c(O_total = length(sets$COG$O), chaperones = length(O_chap), remainder = length(O_nochap))
## MEASURED on the clean knit, 24 Sep 2026: 321 / 264 / 57 on the exploratory
## universe with chap_new. The earlier 248 / 204 / 44 came from a session with
## both the wrong universe and the initial annotation (chap_prot); both are fixed.
## Same decomposition as the reported version (405 / 324 / 81), on the smaller
## exploratory universe.
##
## Composition matters for how "remainder" is read. Within the 204 chaperones:
## GroEL 73, DnaK 48, K13993 28, GrpE 15, GroES 8, K07533 7, then singles. The 44
## remainder proteins are NOT other chaperones — they are thioredoxin (K03671),
## DegP (K04771), peroxiredoxin (K03386), PpiB (K03769), FtsH (K03798) and 8
## unassigned: oxidative-stress and protease functions. "COG O remainder" reads
## as "the other chaperones" and is nothing of the kind, which is why it being
## flat says what it says.

## `stat` is built in §6b from the same FA and is still in scope here. It was
## recomputed at this point with a byte-identical expression, which was harmless
## only by coincidence: §6d, §12e and §13's full-space input all read `stat`
## AFTER this chunk, and `names(stat)` is the multiplicity denominator. Any edit
## to one copy and not the other would have corrupted the discovery universe
## silently. Removed 24 Sep 2026 — use the one definition.
stopifnot(exists("stat"), length(stat) > 1000)
fgseaMultilevel(list(O_nochap = O_nochap, chaperones = O_chap),
                stat, minSize = 10, eps = 0) |>
  tibble::as_tibble() |> dplyr::select(pathway, size, NES, pval)

## What each half contains — the split must be inspected, not assumed.
annot |> dplyr::filter(cohort == "pitt", protein %in% O_nochap) |>
  dplyr::count(ko_primary, sort = TRUE) |> head(10)
annot |> dplyr::filter(cohort == "pitt", protein %in% O_chap) |>
  dplyr::count(ko_primary, sort = TRUE) |> head(10)
```

```{r c3-bacillota-denominator}
## Numerator and denominator both restricted to Bacillota, so the phylum ratio
## divides out.
bac_rows  <- pep_ph$row[pep_ph$tax == "Bacillota"]
chap_rows <- which(OP$rd$Protein %in% chap_new)

num <- colSums(OP$a[intersect(bac_rows, chap_rows), OP$d$sample, drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE)
den <- colSums(OP$a[bac_rows,                        OP$d$sample, drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE)
dd  <- OP$d |> dplyr::mutate(frac = num / den) |>
  dplyr::filter(is.finite(frac), frac > 0, frac < 1)
c(n = nrow(dd), median_frac = median(dd$frac))
summary(lm(qlogis(frac) ~ Mixture + resp, data = dd))

## `pw` (phylum x sample fractions) is built here so C3 is self-contained;
## c10b rebuilds it identically.
pw <- purrr::map_dfr(unique(pep_ph$tax), function(p) {
  idx <- pep_ph$row[pep_ph$tax == p]
  tibble::tibble(phylum = p, sample = OP$d$sample,
                 int = colSums(OP$a[idx, OP$d$sample, drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE))
}) |>
  dplyr::group_by(sample) |> dplyr::mutate(frac = int / sum(int)) |> dplyr::ungroup() |>
  dplyr::select(sample, phylum, frac) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = phylum, values_from = frac, values_fill = 0) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(OP$d |> dplyr::select(sample, Mixture, resp), by = "sample")

## And the phylum ratio as an explicit covariate on the original quantity.
pr <- pw |> dplyr::mutate(lr = log2((Bacteroidota + 1e-6)/(Bacillota + 1e-6))) |>
  dplyr::select(sample, lr)
summary(lm(qlogis(frac) ~ Mixture + lr + resp,
           data = chap_frac_of(OP, chap_new) |> dplyr::inner_join(pr, by = "sample")))
```

```{r c6-matched-control}
## Random sets matched to COG O on SIZE and DETECTION COMPLETENESS — the
## concern is that newly-admitted sparse features carry plex structure.
det <- rowMeans(!is.na(assay(FA$qs, "protein")))
tgt <- det[sets$COG$O]
brk <- quantile(det, seq(0, 1, .2), na.rm = TRUE)
cells <- table(cut(tgt, brk, include.lowest = TRUE))

set.seed(91)
matched_sets <- purrr::map(1:20, function(i) {
  unlist(purrr::imap(cells, function(n, cell) {
    pool <- names(det)[cut(det, brk, include.lowest = TRUE) == cell]
    if (length(pool) < n) pool else sample(pool, n)
  }))
})
names(matched_sets) <- paste0("matched", seq_along(matched_sets))
fgseaMultilevel(matched_sets, stat, minSize = 10, eps = 0) |>
  tibble::as_tibble() |>
  dplyr::summarise(n = dplyr::n(), median_NES = median(NES), min_NES = min(NES),
                   n_p05 = sum(pval < .05))
## MEASURED on the clean knit, 24 Sep 2026: 20 sets, median NES +0.8397, min
## -1.1336, ZERO at nominal p < 0.05 — reproducing the recorded +0.84 / -1.13.
## An earlier diagnostic run gave -0.911 / -1.328 / 3 because the pool is drawn
## against sets$COG$O and that session carried the wrong universe (§6a). With the
## universe correct this check matches the record.
##
## The conclusion: the most extreme of 20 size- and detection-matched random sets
## reaches -1.13 against COG O's -2.24, and none of them clears nominal p < 0.05.
```

```{r c8-host-inflammation}
  dplyr::mutate(inflam   = colMeans(hs[INFL, sample, drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE),
                host_all = colMeans(hs[,     sample, drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  dplyr::filter(is.finite(inflam)) |> droplevels()
nrow(hi)

## 1. Does inflammation itself differ by response?
summary(lm(inflam ~ Mixture + resp, data = hi))

## 2. Within plex — both are plex-structured, so the pooled correlation is
##    confounded (it gave rho = -0.56 against -0.25 within plex).
cor(residuals(lm(qlogis(frac) ~ Mixture, hi)),
    residuals(lm(inflam       ~ Mixture, hi)), method = "spearman")

## 3. Is it compositional? TMT fixes total signal per channel, so ANY host
##    quantity might compete with a microbial fraction. Host TOTAL is the control.
summary(lm(qlogis(frac) ~ Mixture + host_all + resp, data = hi))
summary(lm(qlogis(frac) ~ Mixture + host_all + inflam + resp, data = hi))

## 4. Inflammation as a SHARE of host protein — removes the shared denominator.
hi <- hi |> dplyr::mutate(infl_rel = inflam - host_all)
summary(lm(qlogis(frac) ~ Mixture + infl_rel + resp, data = hi))
```

```{r c10d-within-bacteroides}
## Chaperone fraction of each genus's OWN proteome — within-genus,
## within-channel, so loading, composition and organism abundance divide out.
chap_within <- function(gname, min_psm = 200L) {
  g <- pep_g |> dplyr::filter(tax == gname)
  if (nrow(g) < min_psm) return(tibble::tibble())
  den <- colSums(a[g$row, OP$d$sample, drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE)
  num <- colSums(a[g$row[g$Protein %in% chap_new], OP$d$sample, drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE)
  dd <- OP$d |> dplyr::mutate(frac = num / den) |>
    dplyr::filter(is.finite(frac), frac > 0, frac < 1) |> droplevels()
  if (nrow(dd) < 20 || dplyr::n_distinct(dd$Mixture) < 2) return(tibble::tibble())
  test_frac(dd, gname) |> dplyr::mutate(n_psm = nrow(g),
                                        n_chap = sum(g$Protein %in% chap_new))
}
top_g <- dplyr::count(pep_g, tax, sort = TRUE) |> dplyr::filter(n >= 200) |> dplyr::pull(tax)
purrr::map_dfr(top_g, chap_within) |>
  dplyr::mutate(q = p.adjust(p.value, "BH")) |> dplyr::arrange(p.value) |> as.data.frame()

purrr::map_dfr(top_g, function(gn) {
  g <- pep_g |> dplyr::filter(tax == gn)
  tibble::tibble(genus = gn, n_psm = nrow(g),
                 n_chap = sum(g$Protein %in% chap_new))
}) |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(n_psm)) |> head(15)

pep_ph |> dplyr::mutate(is_chap = Protein %in% chap_new) |>
  dplyr::group_by(phylum = tax) |>
  dplyr::summarise(n = dplyr::n(), n_chap = sum(is_chap),
                   frac = n_chap / n, .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(n)) |> head(6)

## Is it LCA resolution? Family rank gives the same answer if not.
pep_fa |> dplyr::filter(grepl("Bacteroid|Porphyromonad|Rikenell|Prevotell", tax)) |>
  dplyr::group_by(family = tax) |>
  dplyr::summarise(n = dplyr::n(), n_chap = sum(Protein %in% chap_new), .groups = "drop")

## Is it multi-genus ambiguity? 95.7% resolve to one genus if not.
pep_g |> dplyr::filter(Protein %in% chap_new) |>
  dplyr::count(Protein, tax) |> dplyr::count(Protein, name = "n_genera") |>
  dplyr::count(n_genera)
```

**What they return.**

| check | result | measured on |
|---|---|---|
| leading edge, peptide support (C1b) | effect size separates 2.7×, SE only 1.2×; the same peptide support in and out of the edge (median 3; 22.7% against 22.8% single-peptide) — not a precision artefact | initial annotation |
| chaperone removal (C2) | chaperones −2.46, remainder +0.79 | completed; 1,000-draw null (§8a). The nominal version in the chunk is a separate computation on the exploratory universe and does not reproduce these values |
| Bacillota-internal denominator (C3) | −0.102, about half the full-denominator −0.189 (§8e), and not significant: within-plex p = 0.247. The chunk used chap_prot until 23 Sep and returned −0.123; on chap_new it should return the recorded value | completed annotation and taxonomy (§5c) |
| matched random sets (C6) | 20 sets, median NES +0.84, min −1.13 against COG O's −2.22 | initial annotation |
| phylum, within plex (C10b) | Bacteroidota +0.157 (higher in responders), p = 0.116 — same direction as the metagenome | completed taxonomy |
| within genus (C10d) | 20 genera, nothing clears (min q = 0.315) | recorded on the initial taxonomy; the chunk now runs on the completed one (chap_new + rebuilt pep_ph), so it will differ |
| host inflammation (C8) | more inflammatory protein, lower chaperone share: −0.259, p = 0.027; responders trend toward more of it (+0.151, p = 0.177); host **total** irrelevant (p = 0.73) | initial set in this code; the completed set agrees to two decimals |

The p for C3 is a within-plex permutation; the p-values for C8 and C10b are
parametric, from plex-adjusted linear models.

**C3 is the result to carry.** Chaperone peptides are a far larger share of
Bacillota protein than of Bacteroidota protein (C10d), and Bacteroidota lean
toward responders, so part of the per-sample difference is composition:
restricted to Bacillota it halves and is no longer significant. C3 and C8 are
fitted together in §8f — they are independent and they add, leaving about half
the difference unexplained and underpowered.

**Host inflammation predicts the chaperone share better than response does.**
With the inflammatory share in the model, the response coefficient falls from
−0.190 to −0.148 (22%; −0.152 with inflammation as an absolute term) and out of
significance (p = 0.078–0.081). It is not mediation — response → inflammation is
p = 0.177 at n = 55 — and mediation, confounding and collinearity cannot be
separated on these data.

## 8d. Time on treatment (exploratory)

Sampling time is balanced (NR median 9 days, IQR 3–30; R 12 days, IQR 4–31;
within-plex p = 0.79), and all 23 non-responders with a recorded progression date
were sampled before it, so the difference is not an artefact of when patients
were sampled. The chaperone share falls with exposure in responders and is flat
in non-responders; no interaction is significant across five variants
(permutation p = 0.11–0.40). The data lean toward a treatment-emergent difference
without establishing one.

```{r time-on-treatment}
## Needs §2f's pitt-timepoint chunk (jp, pitt_meta, pd) and §5c (chap_new, annot_new).
## Checked by type, not existence: short names are reused across this document.
stopifnot(is.data.frame(jp), all(c("days_before", "BioReplicate", "Sample_collection_date") %in% names(jp)),
          is.data.frame(pitt_meta), all(c("MF_ID", "Prog_date") %in% names(pitt_meta)),
          is.function(pd), is.function(chap_frac_of), is.character(chap_new))
## SNAPSHOT UNDER A UNIQUE NAME. `tot` is reassigned in three later chunks
## (b3-denominators, b7-ambiguity, coupling-noise-ceiling), so by the end of a
## knit it is a numeric vector, not this data frame — and the exposure figure,
## which wants this one, got whichever ran last. Same pattern as stat_pitt.
tot <- jp |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(days_before)) |>
  dplyr::left_join(dplyr::select(pitt_meta, MF_ID, Prog_date), by = c("BioReplicate" = "MF_ID")) |>
  dplyr::transmute(sample, Mixture = droplevels(factor(Mixture)),
                   resp = factor(as.character(resp), levels = RESP_LEVELS),
                   rel = -days_before, exposure = pmax(rel, 0),
                   prog_tp = Sample_progression_timepoint,
                   after_prog = pd(Sample_collection_date) > pd(Prog_date))
## NAME the samples this analysis loses before asserting, so a failure says which
## and not merely how many. 54 of 55 before 13 Oct 2026, MF0017 being the undated
## one; 55 of 55 after, since its date arrived with its identity.
.undated <- setdiff(OP$d$sample, tot$sample)
if (length(.undated))
  message("no usable collection date, so outside the time-on-treatment analysis: ",
          paste(.undated, collapse = ", "))
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(tot$sample), identical(levels(tot$resp), c("NR", "R")), nrow(tot) == nrow(OP$d))

## ---- 1. time on treatment by response ------------------------------------------------
tot |> dplyr::group_by(resp) |>
  dplyr::summarise(n = dplyr::n(), median_days = median(rel), q1 = quantile(rel, 0.25),
                   q3 = quantile(rel, 0.75), on_or_before_start = sum(rel <= 0))
bal_obs <- coef(lm(log1p(exposure) ~ Mixture + resp, tot))[["respR"]]
set.seed(7301)
bal_null <- replicate(1000, {
  rp <- factor(ave(as.character(tot$resp), tot$Mixture, FUN = sample), levels = RESP_LEVELS)
  coef(lm(log1p(tot$exposure) ~ tot$Mixture + rp))[["rpR"]] })
## NAMED AND EXPORTED (13 Oct 2026): the S9A panel printed "balanced within
## plex (p = 0.79)" as a literal, which survived every re-run. The figure reads
## this instead.
tot_balance <- c(respR_on_log1p_exposure = bal_obs,
                 p_within_plex = (1 + sum(abs(bal_null) >= abs(bal_obs))) / 1001)
tot_balance

## ---- 2. samples collected after progression ------------------------------------------
table(resp = tot$resp, collected_after_progression = tot$after_prog, useNA = "ifany")
table(resp = tot$resp, Sample_progression_timepoint = tot$prog_tp, useNA = "ifany")

## ---- 3. chaperone fraction against time on treatment ----------------------------------
gd_p <- annot_new$protein[annot_new$cohort == "pitt" & annot_new$ko_primary %in% c("K04077", "K04043")]
frac_join <- function(prots) chap_frac_of(OP, prots) |> dplyr::select(sample, frac) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(tot, by = "sample")
tot_cf   <- frac_join(chap_new)
tot_nogd <- frac_join(setdiff(chap_new, gd_p))
tot_pre  <- dplyr::filter(tot_cf, !(after_prog %in% TRUE))
stopifnot(nrow(tot_cf) == nrow(tot))   # 54L before 13 Oct 2026
coef(summary(lm(qlogis(frac) ~ Mixture + resp, tot_cf)))["respR", ]    # the gap, ignoring time

fl_test <- function(d, x1, B = 1000, seed = 7302) {      # Freedman-Lane, residuals within plex
  d <- dplyr::filter(d, frac > 0, frac < 1)
  full <- lm(qlogis(frac) ~ Mixture + resp * x, d)
  red  <- lm(qlogis(frac) ~ Mixture + resp + x, d)
  ct <- coef(summary(full)); t_obs <- ct["respR:x", "t value"]
  set.seed(seed)
  t_null <- replicate(B, {
    y <- fitted(red) + ave(resid(red), d$Mixture, FUN = sample)
    coef(summary(lm(y ~ Mixture + resp * x, d)))["respR:x", "t value"] })
  b <- coef(full)[c("respR", "respR:x")]; V <- vcov(full)[names(b), names(b)]
  gap <- function(x0) { g <- c(1, x0); c(sum(b * g), sqrt(drop(t(g) %*% V %*% g))) }
  g0 <- gap(0); g1 <- gap(x1)
  tibble::tibble(n = nrow(d), gap_at_0 = g0[1], se_0 = g0[2], gap_at_median = g1[1], se_median = g1[2],
                 interaction = ct["respR:x", "Estimate"], p_param = ct["respR:x", "Pr(>|t|)"],
                 p_perm = (1 + sum(abs(t_null) >= abs(t_obs))) / (1 + B))
}
med_e <- median(tot_cf$exposure)
tot_variants <- list(
  "PRIMARY: log1p(days)"               = list(d = tot_cf,   x = log1p(tot_cf$exposure),  x1 = log1p(med_e)),
  "days, linear"                       = list(d = tot_cf,   x = tot_cf$exposure,         x1 = med_e),
  "late vs early (median split)"       = list(d = tot_cf,   x = as.numeric(tot_cf$exposure > med_e), x1 = 1),
  "chaperones without GroEL/DnaK"      = list(d = tot_nogd, x = log1p(tot_nogd$exposure), x1 = log1p(med_e)),
  "excluding post-progression samples" = list(d = tot_pre,  x = log1p(tot_pre$exposure),  x1 = log1p(med_e)))
tot_res <- purrr::imap_dfr(tot_variants, function(v, nm) {
  d <- v$d; d$x <- v$x; dplyr::mutate(fl_test(d, v$x1), variant = nm, .before = 1) })
print(as.data.frame(tot_res), digits = 3)
## gap_at_0: R - NR at exposure 0 (the median-split row: early); gap_at_median: at the median
## exposure (median-split row: late). Negative = more chaperone in non-responders.

tot_cf$adj <- resid(lm(qlogis(frac) ~ Mixture, tot_cf))
ggplot(tot_cf, aes(exposure, adj, colour = resp)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = TRUE, linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log1p", breaks = c(0, 3, 10, 30, 100)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(NR = "#D55E00", R = "#0072B2"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Days on treatment at collection (0 = on or before start; log1p scale)",
       y = "logit chaperone fraction, plex-adjusted",
       title = "Chaperone fraction against time on treatment, Pittsburgh") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 9)

## Snapshot for the figures: see the note above.
tot_exposure <- tot
```

## 8e. The chaperone share per sample {#chaperone-share}

The set-level result in units a reader can picture. **Not independent
evidence** — same samples, same discovery. A *share* rather than a sum: TMT
intensities are relative within plex, so a summed chaperone intensity would
carry any global tilt; the share divides it out.
`qlogis(share) ~ plex + response`, response permuted within plex, 10,000 draws.

```{r chaperone-share}
stopifnot(is.function(chap_frac_of), is.character(chap_new), exists("OP"), is.data.frame(annot_new))
gd_p <- annot_new$protein[annot_new$cohort == "pitt" & annot_new$ko_primary %in% c("K04077", "K04043")]
share_of <- function(prots, label) chap_frac_of(OP, prots) |>
  dplyr::transmute(sample, Mixture = droplevels(factor(Mixture)),
                   resp = factor(as.character(resp), levels = RESP_LEVELS), frac, set = label)
sh7k <- dplyr::bind_rows(share_of(chap_new, "all chaperones"),
                         share_of(intersect(chap_new, gd_p), "GroEL + DnaK"),
                         share_of(setdiff(chap_new, gd_p), "other chaperones"))
perm_share <- function(d, B = 10000L, seed = 7401L) {
  d <- dplyr::filter(d, frac > 0, frac < 1)
  obs <- coef(lm(qlogis(frac) ~ Mixture + resp, d))[["respR"]]
  set.seed(seed)
  nl <- replicate(B, {
    rp <- factor(ave(as.character(d$resp), d$Mixture, FUN = sample), levels = RESP_LEVELS)
    coef(lm(qlogis(d$frac) ~ d$Mixture + rp))[["rpR"]] })
  ex <- sum(abs(nl) >= abs(obs)); ci <- binom.test(ex, B)$conf.int
  tibble::tibble(n = nrow(d), median_NR_pct = 100 * median(d$frac[d$resp == "NR"]),
                 median_R_pct = 100 * median(d$frac[d$resp == "R"]), gap_logit = obs,
                 p_perm = (1 + ex) / (1 + B), mc_lo = ci[1], mc_hi = ci[2])
}
tab7k <- sh7k |> dplyr::group_by(set) |> dplyr::group_modify(~ perm_share(.x)) |> dplyr::ungroup()
print(as.data.frame(tab7k), digits = 3)
## gap_logit = R - NR on the logit scale: negative = a larger chaperone share in non-responders
```

| quantity | median NR | median R | R − NR (logit) | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| all chaperones — the tested quantity | `r v(tk7("all chaperones","median_NR_pct"), "10.86", pct=TRUE)` | `r v(tk7("all chaperones","median_R_pct"), "9.70", pct=TRUE)` | `r v(tk7("all chaperones","gap_logit"), "-0.189")` | **`r v(tk7("all chaperones","p_perm"), "0.026")`** |
| GroEL + DnaK — descriptive | `r v(tk7("GroEL + DnaK","median_NR_pct"), "5.98", pct=TRUE)` | `r v(tk7("GroEL + DnaK","median_R_pct"), "5.43", pct=TRUE)` | `r v(tk7("GroEL + DnaK","gap_logit"), "-0.186")` | `r v(tk7("GroEL + DnaK","p_perm"), "0.024")` |
| the other `r v(length(setdiff(CHAPERONE_KO, c("K04077","K04043"))), "17")` chaperones — descriptive | `r v(tk7("other chaperones","median_NR_pct"), "4.31", pct=TRUE)` | `r v(tk7("other chaperones","median_R_pct"), "4.30", pct=TRUE)` | — | `r v(tk7("other chaperones","p_perm"), "0.154")` |

By abundance the difference is GroEL and DnaK, and the other chaperones are
level. By rank (§8a) they lean the same way at nominal significance. The views
differ because a rank statistic weights every protein equally, while a share
weights by abundance, which GroEL and DnaK dominate.

## 8f. Composition and host inflammation, jointly {#joint}

C3 and C8 each remove part of the per-sample difference, and until now neither
had been fitted with the other present. They are **independent**
(`cor(lr, infl_rel) = +0.05`) and their effects **add**:

```{r joint-adjustment}
## Freedman-Lane: the reduced model's residuals permuted within plex, which is
## the right test when the covariates are themselves associated with response.
pwide <- purrr::map_dfr(unique(pep_ph$tax), function(p) {
  idx <- pep_ph$row[pep_ph$tax == p]
  tibble::tibble(phylum = p, sample = OP$d$sample,
                 int = colSums(OP$a[idx, OP$d$sample, drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE))
}) |> dplyr::group_by(sample) |> dplyr::mutate(frac = int / sum(int)) |> dplyr::ungroup() |>
  dplyr::select(sample, phylum, frac) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = phylum, values_from = frac, values_fill = 0)

d <- chap_frac_of(OP, chap_new) |>
  dplyr::mutate(inflam   = colMeans(hs[INFL, sample, drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE),
                host_all = colMeans(hs[,     sample, drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE),
                infl_rel = inflam - host_all) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(pwide |> dplyr::transmute(sample,
                      lr = log2((Bacteroidota + 1e-6) / (Bacillota + 1e-6))), by = "sample") |>
  dplyr::filter(is.finite(frac), frac > 0, frac < 1, is.finite(infl_rel), is.finite(lr)) |>
  droplevels()
c(n = nrow(d), overlap = cor(d$lr, d$infl_rel, method = "spearman"))

fl <- function(covars, dat, seed, B = 2000) {
  rhs  <- paste(c("Mixture", covars), collapse = " + ")
  full <- lm(as.formula(paste("qlogis(frac) ~", rhs, "+ resp")), data = dat)
  red  <- lm(as.formula(paste("qlogis(frac) ~", rhs)),            data = dat)
  obs  <- coef(summary(full))["respR", 1]
  e <- residuals(red); f <- fitted(red); set.seed(seed)
  nl <- replicate(B, {
    dd <- dat; dd$.y <- f + e[ave(seq_along(e), dat$Mixture, FUN = sample)]
    coef(summary(lm(as.formula(paste(".y ~", rhs, "+ resp")), data = dd)))["respR", 1]
  })
  c(resp = obs, se = coef(summary(full))["respR", 2],
    p_perm = (1 + sum(abs(nl) >= abs(obs))) / (1 + B))
}
JA <- rbind(none = fl(character(0), d, 7101), lr = fl("lr", d, 7102),
      infl = fl("infl_rel", d, 7103), both = fl(c("lr","infl_rel"), d, 7104),
      both_host = fl(c("lr","infl_rel","host_all"), d, 7105))
JA

di <- DC3 |> dplyr::inner_join(d |> dplyr::select(sample, infl_rel, host_all), by = "sample") |>
  dplyr::filter(is.finite(frac), frac > 0, frac < 1) |> droplevels()
JAI <- rbind(internal = fl(character(0), di, 7201), internal_infl = fl("infl_rel", di, 7202))
JAI
## EXPECTED (n = 55): none -0.1893 p 0.027 | lr -0.1311 (0.075) | infl -0.1483
##   (0.071) | both -0.0989 (0.176) | both+host -0.0979 (0.188); overlap +0.051.
##   Bacillota-internal: -0.1019 (0.272); with infl_rel -0.0571 (0.519).
##   R2: plex 0.761 | +resp 0.784 | +lr 0.834 | +infl 0.792 | +both 0.854.
```

| adjustment | resp | permutation p | retained |
|---|---|---|---|
| none | `r v(jav("none","resp"), "-0.189")` | `r v(jav("none","p_perm"), "0.027")` | `r v(jav("none","resp")/jav("none","resp"), "1.00")` |
| composition (`lr`) | `r v(jav("lr","resp"), "-0.131")` | `r v(jav("lr","p_perm"), "0.075")` | `r v(jav("lr","resp")/jav("none","resp"), "0.69")` |
| host inflammation (`infl_rel`) | `r v(jav("infl","resp"), "-0.148")` | `r v(jav("infl","p_perm"), "0.071")` | `r v(jav("infl","resp")/jav("none","resp"), "0.78")` |
| **both** | **`r v(jav("both","resp"), "-0.099")`** | **`r v(jav("both","p_perm"), "0.176")`** | **`r v(jav("both","resp")/jav("none","resp"), "0.52")`** |
| both, plus total host protein | `r v(jav("both_host","resp"), "-0.098")` | `r v(jav("both_host","p_perm"), "0.188")` | `r v(jav("both_host","resp")/jav("none","resp"), "0.52")` |

The restriction route agrees: on the Bacillota-internal fraction the coefficient
is −0.102, and −0.057 with the inflammatory share added.

About **half** the per-sample difference is composition and host inflammatory
protein, acting through separate channels. The residual is −0.099 with a 95%
interval of roughly −0.24 to +0.04, so half is not distinguishable from nothing
at this size — underpowered, not absent. Plex alone explains **76%** of the
variance in the chaperone share; response adds 2.3 points unadjusted and 0.6
after both covariates.

## 8g. Denominators, composition and host state — the September 22 follow-ups {#followups}

Four analyses run after the null series, each in a companion script listed in the
Appendix. They qualify §8a–§8f rather than extend them.

**Abundance specificity** (`B9_abundance_tilt.R`). Against 1,000 sets matched to
the chaperone set on abundance-decile composition and size, the null is centred on
zero (median −0.0003, 95% −0.088 to +0.092) and both real sets sit outside every
draw (chaperones −0.189, ribosomal −0.173; percentile 0, p = 0.001 = the 1,000-draw
floor). No tilt to adjust for: detected count, top-100, top-500 and Gini all
p = 0.15–0.47 by response, and adjusting leaves −0.162 and −0.184. Note the
share-based sets carry every annotated member in the PSM assay (568 and 1,320)
against §6b's universe-intersected 393 and 928.

**Per-KO coupling** (`B2_paired_layer_formal.R`, `B10_per_ko_slopes.R`,
`B11_out_of_sample_coupling.R`). KO identity explains 0.75092 of the variance in
log protein share across 32,912 patient-KO observations; own gene abundance adds
+0.00010, patient identity +0.00675. Out of sample, on a baseline of KO mean plus
mean capacity (median R² 0.759), own capacity deviation beats a stranger's in 30
of 47 patients by a median +0.00013, p = 0.064 — leave-two-out, so neither
patient is in the training fit. Positive, underdetermined, negligible either
way.
Per KO the slopes are displaced from a pairing-shuffled null (median +0.0074
against +0.0004, p = 0.015 at 200 permutations; positive in 55.1% against 49.7%,
p = 0.060) but negligible in size — a doubling of gene abundance moves protein by
about half a percent. Slope does not track gene variability (ρ = −0.09), in
tension with the variability-bin result, and the largest slopes rest on the
fewest patients.

**Denominators** (`B3_chaperone_denominators.R`). The response coefficient on the
chaperone share depends on what it is divided by: all microbial protein −0.189
(p = 0.026); Bacillota protein only −0.102 (p = 0.266, matching C3); chaperone
against chaperone-plus-ribosomal −0.023 (p = 0.758). The ribosomal share alone is
−0.173 (p = 0.015). Chaperones do not move relative to translation.

**Composition against expression** (`B4b_composition_partition_fixed.R`). Genus
chaperone propensity estimated leave-one-patient-out, each patient's predicted
share and residual tested separately. Restricting to the 29 assignable genera
costs a fifth of the effect (−0.16, p ≈ 0.17) before any partition. With
proteome-derived composition the split is 27% / 73%, neither significant; with
metagenome-derived composition the prediction anti-tracks the observed share
(r = −0.49) and the partition is not readable. Not estimable at this size.

**Host state** (`B5_host_external_score.R`). A response-blind PC1 of the host
proteome (15.3% of variance) carries the inverse association at a smaller p-value
than the curated panel: 0.00098 against 0.032, surviving adjustment for total
microbial signal (p = 0.00083). The coefficients −0.041 and −0.233 sit on
differently scaled predictors — component units against a mean intensity score —
so the p-values compare and the coefficients do not. Its largest loadings are
brush-border, enterocyte and pancreatic proteins; that is a loading pattern to
interpret, not a measurement of barrier function, and the component is diffuse
(top loadings ≈0.15 where a uniform axis over 147 proteins gives 0.08). The
response coefficient falls out of significance under the panel (−0.154, p = 0.067)
but not under PC1 (−0.174, p = 0.026) — so the stronger predictor of the
chaperone share removes less of the response association, which is why no single
host quantity accounts for it.

**Where the coupling fails** (`B6_decoupling_cause.R`, `B6b_label_check.R`,
`B7_mapping_ambiguity.R`, `B8_family_arbiter.R`). Within patients, every phylum's
proteomic abundance tracks its metagenomic abundance except Bacteroidota: on
centred log-ratios Actinomycetota +0.32, Bacillota +0.20, Pseudomonadota +0.18,
Bacteroidota −0.03. Across 17 families, Bacillota median +0.34 and Bacteroidota
−0.08 (CLR +0.31 against +0.10), Actinomycetota families highest at +0.60;
Prevotellaceae is the one Bacteroidota family that couples (+0.27). At genus
level Bacillota reach 0.3–0.7 and Bacteroidota ≈ 0. Excluded: closure (CLR at
every level), evidence depth (Bacteroidota mid-range at 1,132 PSM rows per genus,
poorer genera couple), nomenclature (4 of 5 genera self-matching against 15 of 22),
and assignment (genus resolution 52.6% against 50.5%; multi-genus ambiguity 3.2%
against 2.3%; genus-assigned part tracks the whole clade at ρ = 0.99 in both).
The search database is the last technical explanation standing.

A correction worth recording: an earlier version of this test compared the two
clades at phylum level over two components only. Closure made both clades look
uncoupled (−0.18 and −0.09), and the verdict rule asked whether Bacteroidota was
flat without requiring the control clade to couple, so it passed on a test that
had lost its contrast. Every comparison above reports the control clade.

```{r b3-denominators}
local({
  ## B3 — is the chaperone signal specific, or a readout of biomass/composition?
  ## The ribosomal set gives a nearly identical paired-model coefficient, so the
  ## question a reviewer will ask is whether chaperones move relative to general
  ## protein output at all. Tested against four denominators, including translation.
  ## Run after §8 (needs §5c).

  B <- 2000

  sum_rows <- function(prots) colSums(OP$a[which(OP$rd$Protein %in% prots), OP$d$sample, drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE)
  tot  <- colSums(OP$a[, OP$d$sample, drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE)
  bac  <- colSums(OP$a[pep_ph$row[pep_ph$tax == "Bacillota"], OP$d$sample, drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE)
  chap <- sum_rows(chap_new); ribo <- sum_rows(ribo_new)
  bac_chap <- colSums(OP$a[intersect(pep_ph$row[pep_ph$tax == "Bacillota"],
                                     which(OP$rd$Protein %in% chap_new)), OP$d$sample, drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE)

  D <- list(
    `all microbial protein`      = chap / tot,
    `Bacillota protein only`     = bac_chap / bac,
    `ribosomal protein`          = chap / (chap + ribo),   # chaperone share of chaperone+translation
    `ribosomal, as a log ratio`  = NA)                     # handled below
  fit1 <- function(v, logratio = FALSE) {
    d <- OP$d |> mutate(y = if (logratio) v else qlogis(v)) |> filter(is.finite(y)) |> droplevels()
    o <- coef(summary(lm(y ~ Mixture + resp, d)))["respR", 1]
    set.seed(8801)
    nl <- replicate(B, {
      rp <- factor(ave(as.character(d$resp), d$Mixture, FUN = sample), levels = levels(d$resp))
      coef(summary(lm(d$y ~ d$Mixture + rp)))[grep("^rp", rownames(coef(summary(lm(d$y ~ d$Mixture + rp))))), 1]
    })
    c(n = nrow(d), resp = o, p_two = (1 + sum(abs(nl) >= abs(o))) / (1 + B))
  }
  out <- rbind(
    `chaperone / all microbial`        = fit1(D[["all microbial protein"]]),
    `chaperone / Bacillota`            = fit1(D[["Bacillota protein only"]]),
    `chaperone / (chaperone+ribosomal)`= fit1(D[["ribosomal protein"]]),
    ## `log(chap/ribo)` is IDENTICALLY qlogis(chap/(chap+ribo)) — the row above —
  ## so reporting both read as two confirmations when it is one quantity. Kept
  ## as a single row; the identity is noted rather than re-printed.
    `ribosomal / all microbial`        = fit1(ribo / tot))
  cat("\nresponse coefficient under each denominator (within-plex permutation)\n")
  print(round(out, 4))
  cat("\n READING: the chaperone-to-translation ratio is FLAT\n",
      " while both shares move against all microbial protein, so this is\n",
      " not selective chaperone induction. It is also NOT a generic\n",
      " abundance effect: B9's abundance-matched sets are centred on zero\n",
      " and both real sets fall outside all 1,000 draws. What moves is the\n",
      " chaperone-and-translation fraction as a unit (§2.2).\n")
})
  ## EXPECTED (n = 55): chaperone/all microbial -0.1893 (p 0.0255);
  ##   chaperone/Bacillota -0.1019 (0.2659); chaperone/(chaperone+ribosomal)
  ##   -0.0226 (0.7581); log(chaperone/ribosomal) identical to it by construction;
  ##   ribosomal/all microbial -0.1725 (0.0145).
```

```{r b5-host-scores}
local({
  ## B5 — re-score the host association without a hand-picked panel.
  ## The nine-protein panel is biologically coherent but was assembled by us, so it
  ## is open to the charge of being curated around the result. Two response-blind
  ## alternatives: an externally defined gene set, and the first principal component
  ## of the host proteome. Neither uses the response label in its construction.
  ##
  ## Optional: HOST_SET_FILE, one gene symbol or UniProt ENTRY name per line, e.g.
  ## Reactome R-HSA-6798695 "Neutrophil degranulation" exported as gene symbols.
  ## Run after §8 (needs hs, INFL, chap_frac_of, chap_new).

  base <- chap_frac_of(OP, chap_new) |> filter(is.finite(frac), frac > 0, frac < 1)
  H <- hs[, base$sample, drop = FALSE]
  H <- H[rowSums(is.finite(H)) >= 0.8 * ncol(H), , drop = FALSE]
  cat(sprintf("host proteins with >=80%% coverage: %d over %d samples\n", nrow(H), ncol(H)))

  ## response-blind summary 1: first PCs of the host proteome.
  ## prcomp treats ROWS as observations, so the matrix handed to it must be
  ## samples x proteins — not the protein x sample orientation H is stored in.
  X <- H[complete.cases(H), , drop = FALSE]                 # proteins x samples
  X <- X[apply(X, 1, sd) > 0, , drop = FALSE]               # scale() needs non-zero variance
  Z <- scale(t(X))                                          # samples x proteins
  stopifnot(nrow(Z) == ncol(X), identical(rownames(Z), colnames(X)))
  pc <- prcomp(Z, center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE)
  stopifnot(nrow(pc$x) == nrow(Z))
  base$host_pc1 <- pc$x[match(base$sample, rownames(pc$x)), 1]   # keyed, not positional
  base$host_pc2 <- pc$x[match(base$sample, rownames(pc$x)), 2]
  panel <- colMeans(hs[INFL, base$sample, drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE)
  cat(sprintf("PCA on %d samples x %d proteins; PC1 %.1f%% of variance, PC2 %.1f%%; cor(PC1, curated panel) = %+.2f\n",
              nrow(Z), ncol(Z), 100 * summary(pc)$importance[2, 1],
              100 * summary(pc)$importance[2, 2], cor(base$host_pc1, panel)))

  ## response-blind summary 2: an external set, if supplied
  ext <- NULL
  if (exists("HOST_SET_FILE") && file.exists(HOST_SET_FILE)) {
    g <- toupper(trimws(readLines(HOST_SET_FILE, warn = FALSE))); g <- g[nzchar(g)]
    rn <- toupper(rownames(H)); hit <- rn %in% g | sub("_HUMAN$", "", rn) %in% g
    cat(sprintf("external set: %d of %d names matched host rows\n", sum(hit), length(g)))
    if (sum(hit) >= 5) ext <- colMeans(H[hit, , drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE)
  } else message("HOST_SET_FILE not set — PC route only. Export Reactome R-HSA-6798695 to add it.")
  if (!is.null(ext)) base$host_ext <- ext[base$sample]

  fit <- function(v, lab) {
    d <- base |> mutate(h = v) |> filter(is.finite(h))
    cf <- coef(summary(lm(qlogis(frac) ~ Mixture + h + resp, d)))
    data.frame(score = lab, n = nrow(d), host_coef = cf["h", 1], host_p = cf["h", 4],
               resp_coef = cf["respR", 1], resp_p = cf["respR", 4])
  }
  rows <- list(fit(colMeans(hs[INFL, base$sample, drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE), "curated 9-protein panel"),
               fit(base$host_pc1, "host PC1 (response-blind)"),
               fit(base$host_pc2, "host PC2 (response-blind)"))
  if (!is.null(ext)) rows <- c(rows, list(fit(base$host_ext, "external neutrophil set")))
  res <- do.call(rbind, rows)
  cat("\nchaperone share on host score and response, within plex\n"); print(res, row.names = FALSE, digits = 3)
})
  ## EXPECTED: 220 host proteins at >=80% coverage, 147 complete. PCA 55 samples x
  ##   147 proteins; PC1 15.3% of variance, PC2 8.6%; cor(PC1, curated panel) +0.23.
  ##   Chaperone share on host score and response: curated panel host -0.2329
  ##   (p 0.032), resp -0.154 (0.067); PC1 host -0.0412 (0.00098), resp -0.174
  ##   (0.026); PC2 host +0.0023 (0.86), resp -0.191 (0.030). PC1 loads brush-border
  ##   and pancreatic proteins, not the inflammatory panel.
```

```{r b9-abundance-tilt}
local({
  ## B9 — is the housekeeping-fraction shift an abundance tilt?
  ##
  ## Motivation, as it stood when this was written: §2.2 had the chaperone share
  ## at -0.189 (p = 0.026) and the ribosomal share at -0.173 (p = 0.015) with the
  ## ratio flat, and read that as a shift in the abundant housekeeping fraction.
  ## If non-responder samples are more top-heavy — a larger share of intensity in
  ## the most abundant proteins, or fewer proteins detected — then the share of ANY
  ## abundant class rises mechanically. C6 matched random sets on size and detection
  ## completeness, never on abundance rank, so this has never been tested and it
  ## underpins the section's new wording.
  ##
  ## Three parts:
  ##   TILT      does top-heaviness itself differ by response, within plex
  ##   ADJUST    how much of the chaperone coefficient survives with tilt in the model
  ##   MATCHED   1,000 random sets matched to the chaperone set on abundance-decile
  ##             composition AND size — where do the real sets fall in that null?
  ##
  ## The MATCHED test is the one that decides what §2.2 may claim. Run after §8.

  set.seed(9901); B <- 2000; NSET <- 1000L
  S <- OP$d$sample; A <- OP$a[, S, drop = FALSE]; tot <- colSums(A, na.rm = TRUE)

  rows_of <- split(seq_len(nrow(A)), OP$rd$Protein)
  prot_tot <- vapply(rows_of, function(r) sum(A[r, ], na.rm = TRUE), 0)
  prot_tot <- prot_tot[is.finite(prot_tot) & prot_tot > 0]
  dec <- cut(rank(-prot_tot), breaks = quantile(rank(-prot_tot), seq(0, 1, .1)),
             include.lowest = TRUE, labels = paste0("D", 1:10))   # D1 = most abundant
  names(dec) <- names(prot_tot)

  share_of <- function(prots) {
    r <- unlist(rows_of[intersect(prots, names(rows_of))], use.names = FALSE)
    colSums(A[r, , drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE) / tot
  }
  perm_coef <- function(y, dat = OP$d, seed = 9902) {
    d <- dat |> mutate(yy = y) |> filter(is.finite(yy)) |> droplevels()
    o <- coef(summary(lm(yy ~ Mixture + resp, d)))["respR", 1]; set.seed(seed)
    nl <- replicate(B, { rp <- factor(ave(as.character(d$resp), d$Mixture, FUN = sample),
                                      levels = levels(d$resp))
      cf <- coef(summary(lm(d$yy ~ d$Mixture + rp))); cf[grep("^rp", rownames(cf)), 1] })
    c(coef = o, p_two = (1 + sum(abs(nl) >= abs(o))) / (1 + B))
  }

  ## ---- 1. does the tilt itself differ by response? ----------------------------
  psum <- vapply(rows_of, function(r) colSums(A[r, , drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE), numeric(length(S)))
  topn <- function(k) apply(psum, 1, function(v) sum(sort(v, decreasing = TRUE)[1:k], na.rm = TRUE) / sum(v, na.rm = TRUE))
  gini <- apply(psum, 1, function(v) { v <- sort(v[v > 0]); n <- length(v)
    sum((2 * seq_len(n) - n - 1) * v) / (n * sum(v)) })
  tilt <- tibble(sample = S, n_detected = colSums(!is.na(A)),
                 top100 = topn(100), top500 = topn(500), gini = gini)
  cat("[1] top-heaviness by response, within plex\n")
  print(round(rbind(n_detected = perm_coef(tilt$n_detected),
                    top100     = perm_coef(qlogis(tilt$top100)),
                    top500     = perm_coef(qlogis(tilt$top500)),
                    gini       = perm_coef(tilt$gini)), 4))

  ## ---- 2. the chaperone coefficient with the tilt in the model ----------------
  d2 <- OP$d |> mutate(y = qlogis(share_of(chap_new)), t100 = qlogis(tilt$top100),
                       nd = scale(tilt$n_detected)[, 1]) |> filter(is.finite(y))
  cf <- function(f) coef(summary(lm(as.formula(f), d2)))["respR", c(1, 4)]
  cat(sprintf("\n[2] chaperone share: unadjusted %+.4f (p %.3f) | + top100 %+.4f (p %.3f) | + n_detected %+.4f (p %.3f)\n",
              cf("y ~ Mixture + resp")[1], cf("y ~ Mixture + resp")[2],
              cf("y ~ Mixture + t100 + resp")[1], cf("y ~ Mixture + t100 + resp")[2],
              cf("y ~ Mixture + nd + resp")[1], cf("y ~ Mixture + nd + resp")[2]))

  ## ---- 3. abundance-matched random sets ---------------------------------------
  matched_null <- function(prots, lab) {
    p <- intersect(prots, names(dec)); prof <- table(dec[p])
    obs <- perm_coef(qlogis(share_of(p)))[["coef"]]
    nl <- vapply(seq_len(NSET), function(i) {
      pick <- unlist(lapply(names(prof), function(dd) {
        pool <- setdiff(names(dec)[dec == dd], p)
        sample(pool, min(prof[[dd]], length(pool)))
      }), use.names = FALSE)
      coef(summary(lm(qlogis(share_of(pick)) ~ OP$d$Mixture + OP$d$resp)))[
        grep("^OP\\$d\\$resp", rownames(coef(summary(lm(qlogis(share_of(pick)) ~ OP$d$Mixture + OP$d$resp))))), 1]
    }, 0)
    tibble(set = lab, n_prot = length(p), observed = obs,
           null_median = median(nl), null_lo = quantile(nl, .025), null_hi = quantile(nl, .975),
           pctile = mean(nl <= obs), p_two = (1 + sum(abs(nl) >= abs(obs))) / (1 + NSET))
  }
  mt <- bind_rows(matched_null(chap_new, "chaperones"), matched_null(ribo_new, "ribosomal"))
  cat("\n[3] against 1,000 random sets matched on abundance decile and size\n")
  print(as.data.frame(mt), row.names = FALSE, digits = 3)

  generic <- abs(mt$null_median[1]) > 0.5 * abs(mt$observed[1])
  tilted  <- perm_coef(qlogis(tilt$top100))[["p_two"]] < 0.05
  cat("\n---- verdict ----\n", if (generic)
  "GENERIC. Abundance-matched random sets shift by about as much as the real ones,
  so non-responders carry a higher share of abundant protein in general. §2.2 must
  say that: chaperones and ribosomal protein are instances of a global tilt, not a
  property of those classes. Every share-based coefficient in the paper inherits
  this and should be reported against the matched null, not against zero." else if (tilted)
  "TILTED BUT NOT GENERIC. Top-heaviness differs by response, yet abundance-matched
  sets do not reproduce the shift. Report the tilt as a covariate and give the
  chaperone coefficient adjusted for it." else
  "SPECIFIC. Neither top-heaviness nor abundance-matched sets account for it: the
  shift is in these abundant classes, not in abundant protein generally. §2.2's
  wording stands, and this control belongs beside C6 as the abundance-matched
  companion to the size- and detection-matched one.", "\n")
})
  ## EXPECTED: tilt by response all null — n_detected p 0.469, top100 0.299,
  ##   top500 0.202, Gini 0.155. Chaperone share -0.1893 unadjusted, -0.1619 with
  ##   top100, -0.1843 with detected count. Abundance-matched nulls centred on zero
  ##   (median -0.0003, 95% -0.088 to +0.092); chaperones -0.189 and ribosomal
  ##   -0.173 lie outside all 1,000 draws (percentile 0, p 0.001 = the floor).
```

---

# 9. Measurement properties of the design {#measurement}

On the 75-sample matrix, which includes the two dropped plexes, many sets peak
in TMT1/TMT2. `spread` (max − min of per-plex medians) is
size-dependent and outlier-sensitive, so it is judged against a **size-matched
null** with the same NA exposure as the observed scan; draws where a random set
is unobserved in an entire plex are discarded and the discard rate reported per
size. A robust `sd` alternative is computed alongside. COG O itself carries an
offset (spread 0.316): lowest in TMT1/TMT2 (−0.108, −0.062) against +0.024 to
+0.208 elsewhere. The permutation is within plex, so every draw carries the same
offsets; an offset alone cannot produce a response contrast under the null.

Re-scored with a 1,000-draw null and BH across sets: of the 60 pathway sets, 24
carry an offset at q < 0.10 where 3 are expected. Excluding the 13 KEGG global
maps, which are offset by construction, **21 of 53 sets — in 16 of 42 groups at
Jaccard < 0.5 — exceed a size-matched null**, 15 of them at q < 0.05. They lean
toward the two plexes with the most unbalanced response composition (16 of 21
peak in TMT1/TMT2; OR 3.5, Fisher p = 0.048, 95% CI 0.94–15.5), on a matrix that
passes every global quality check. The outlier-sensitivity objection does not
bind: `spread` and the robust `sd` rank the sets at ρ = 0.986.

```{r plex-offset-scan}
pm <- mp$pitt_mat_f
d  <- limma_da(pm, mp$pitt_annot_use, conditioned = TRUE)$sm
base <- colMeans(pm[, d$Sample], na.rm = TRUE)

set_offset <- function(prots) {
  p <- intersect(prots, rownames(pm)); if (length(p) < 5) return(NULL)
  tapply(colMeans(pm[p, d$Sample, drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE) - base,
         d$Mixture, median)
}
round(rbind(whole   = tapply(colMeans(pm[, d$Sample], na.rm = TRUE), d$Mixture, median),
            COG_O    = set_offset(cog_prot("O")),
            ribosomal= set_offset(ko_prot(RIBO_KO))), 3)

## ---- the 60-set scan --------------------------------------------------------
## `spread` is NA whenever ANY plex has no observation of the set. Recorded
## explicitly rather than allowed to vanish from a `sum(spread > 0.5)`.
off <- dplyr::distinct(mp$pitt_pw_map_obs, Pathway, ProteinID) |>
  dplyr::filter(ProteinID %in% rownames(pm)) |>
  dplyr::group_by(Pathway) |> dplyr::filter(dplyr::n() >= 10) |>
  dplyr::group_modify(~{
    pl <- set_offset(.x$ProteinID)
    ok <- !is.null(pl) && length(pl) == 8L && all(is.finite(pl))
    tibble::tibble(n_prot = nrow(.x),
                   n_plex_obs = if (is.null(pl)) 0L else sum(is.finite(pl)),
                   spread = if (ok) max(pl) - min(pl) else NA_real_,
                   top    = if (ok) names(sort(pl, decreasing = TRUE))[1] else NA_character_)
  }) |> dplyr::ungroup()

c(n = nrow(off),
  complete_8plex = sum(!is.na(off$spread)),
  incomplete     = sum(is.na(off$spread)),
  over_0.5       = sum(off$spread > 0.5, na.rm = TRUE))
dplyr::count(dplyr::filter(off, !is.na(spread), spread > 0.5), top)

## ---- `spread` needs a null ---------------------------------------------------
## Without one, the 0.5 cut is arbitrary. `max - min` is the most
## outlier-sensitive statistic available, and per-plex medians are noisier for
## small sets — so spread is SIZE-DEPENDENT across a scan spanning 10 to 591
## members. A size-matched null and an sd-based robust alternative follow.
##
## The null has the same NA exposure as the observed scan: a random set of n
## proteins can be unobserved in an entire plex. Those draws are DISCARDED and
## the discard rate reported per size — a size where the null is not estimable
## is a size where the statistic is unstable, which is itself the point.
## Returns a LIST, not an attributed matrix: subsetting a matrix drops its
## attributes, which returns a length-0 result rather than an error.
size_matched_null <- function(n_prot, B = 200) {
  out <- replicate(B, {
    pl <- set_offset(sample(rownames(pm), n_prot))
    if (is.null(pl) || length(pl) != 8L || !all(is.finite(pl)))
      return(c(spread = NA_real_, sd = NA_real_))
    c(spread = max(pl) - min(pl), sd = sd(pl))
  })
  ok <- is.finite(out["spread", ])
  list(draws = out[, ok, drop = FALSE], usable = mean(ok), n_ok = sum(ok))
}

set.seed(931)
nullspread <- off |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(spread)) |>
  dplyr::distinct(n_prot) |>
  dplyr::mutate(nl      = purrr::map(n_prot, size_matched_null),
                n_draws = purrr::map_int(nl, "n_ok"),
                usable  = purrr::map_dbl(nl, "usable"),
                q95     = purrr::map_dbl(nl, function(x)
                            if (x$n_ok < 50L) NA_real_ else
                              unname(quantile(x$draws["spread", ], .95)))) |>
  dplyr::select(-nl)

## Sizes where the null could not be estimated — fewer than 50 usable draws.
nullspread |> dplyr::filter(is.na(q95) | usable < 0.8) |> as.data.frame()
c(sizes = nrow(nullspread), estimable = sum(!is.na(nullspread$q95)),
  min_usable = min(nullspread$usable))

off2 <- off |> dplyr::left_join(nullspread, by = "n_prot") |>
  dplyr::mutate(exceeds_null = spread > q95)          # NA where either is NA
c(n = nrow(off2),
  over_0.5                  = sum(off2$spread > 0.5, na.rm = TRUE),
  exceeds_size_matched_null = sum(off2$exceeds_null, na.rm = TRUE),
  not_assessable            = sum(is.na(off2$exceeds_null)))
dplyr::count(dplyr::filter(off2, !is.na(exceeds_null) & exceeds_null), top)

## THE OFFSET CLAIM'S OWN SETS: of the sets peaking in TMT1/TMT2, how many
## of those are assessable against the null at all? If several are not, the
## claim rests on fewer sets than stated — and that must be visible.
claim_sets <- off2 |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(spread), spread > 0.5,
                                    top %in% c("TMT1","TMT2"))
c(claimed          = nrow(claim_sets),
  assessable       = sum(!is.na(claim_sets$exceeds_null)),
  exceed_null      = sum(claim_sets$exceeds_null, na.rm = TRUE),
  median_n_prot    = median(claim_sets$n_prot))

## And the robust alternative. If `spread` and `sd` rank the sets the same way,
## the outlier-sensitivity objection does not bind in practice.
off3 <- off2 |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(spread)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(sd_based = purrr::map_dbl(Pathway, function(p) {
    pl <- set_offset(prot_of(p))
    if (is.null(pl) || !all(is.finite(pl))) NA_real_ else sd(pl)
  }))
c(rho = cor(off3$spread, off3$sd_based, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs"),
  n   = sum(!is.na(off3$sd_based)))

## MEASURED 23 Sep 2026, reproducing the record (60 sets, 35 over 0.5,
## spread-vs-sd rho 0.986, 41 sizes all estimable, min usable 0.995) and adding
## two figures that were not recorded:
##   - 26 of 60 sets exceed a SIZE-MATCHED null, not 35. The raw over_0.5 count
##     includes sets whose offsets are consistent with size alone.
##   - of the 28 claimed sets, 17 exceed that null; median 20.5 proteins.
##   - the offsets are NOT evenly spread: of 35 sets with a top plex, 15 are TMT1
##     and 13 TMT2 (80% in two of eight); the second table gives 13 and 7. TMT2
##     is excluded by the 2/2 rule (9 NR / 1 R), so its offsets never reach a
##     result. TMT1 does, and carries 15 of the 35.
## Both additions strengthen §9: the offsets are real, localised, and half the
## localisation sits in a plex the analysis drops.
```

```{r plex-offset-rescore}
## Per-set empirical p from the size-matched null, BH across sets, the global
## maps excluded, and the redundancy of the remaining sets stated.
## (A3_plex_offset_rescore.R writes the per-set table.)
GLOBAL_MAPS <- paste0("map0", c(1100,1110,1120,1200,1210,1212,1220,1230,1232,1240,1250,1310,1320))
f  <- file.path(paths$out_dir, "A3_plex_offsets", "plex_offset_rescore.csv")
if (!file.exists(f)) stop("run A3_plex_offset_rescore.R first: ", f)
sc <- read.csv(f)
y  <- subset(sc, !Pathway %in% GLOBAL_MAPS)
c(all_sets = nrow(sc), q10_all = sum(sc$q_spread < 0.10, na.rm = TRUE),
  sets = nrow(y), q10 = sum(y$q_spread < 0.10, na.rm = TRUE),
  q05 = sum(y$q_spread < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
  in_NR_heavy = sum(y$q_spread < 0.10 & y$top %in% c("TMT1","TMT2"), na.rm = TRUE))
tab <- table(offset = ifelse(y$q_spread < 0.10, "q<0.10", "ns"),
             peaks  = ifelse(y$top %in% c("TMT1","TMT2"), "TMT1/TMT2", "other"))
tab; fisher.test(tab)

## how many of the 53 are independent?
pp <- dplyr::distinct(mp$pitt_pw_map_obs, Pathway, ProteinID)
S  <- split(pp$ProteinID, pp$Pathway)[y$Pathway]
J  <- vapply(seq_along(S), function(j) vapply(seq_along(S), function(i)
        length(intersect(S[[i]], S[[j]])) / length(union(S[[i]], S[[j]])), 0), numeric(length(S)))
cl <- cutree(hclust(as.dist(1 - J), method = "average"), h = 0.5)
c(groups = length(unique(cl)), groups_with_a_hit = length(unique(cl[y$q_spread < 0.10])))
## EXPECTED: 60 sets, all assessable; 25 exceed the old q95 rule; 24 at q<0.10.
##   Without the global maps: 53 sets, 42 groups, 21 hits in 16 groups, 15 at
##   q<0.05, 16 of 21 peaking in TMT1/TMT2 (OR 3.54, Fisher p = 0.048).
##   spread vs robust sd: rho = 0.986.
```
